Why The Milagro Beanfield War Still Matters Today

Robert Redford's The Milagro Beanfield War shows how one man's decision to water his field sparks a community uprising. This beloved 1988 film blends magical realism, authentic Latino characters, and environmental themes in ways that feel even more relevant today than when it was released.

30 April 2025 · RewindZone Archive

The first time I watched Robert Redford's The Milagro Beanfield War, I was hooked!

This is a movie about a guy watering a bean field? Somehow, it works!

And that's exactly why this film still matters today—it shows how one simple act can spark a movement that speaks to issues we still face.

This 1988 gem has only gotten more relevant with time. What started as a charming underdog story now feels almost prophetic in how it portrays struggles over water, land, and community identity. While blockbusters from that era feel dated, Redford's small-town tale speaks to today's headlines in ways that make it worth revisiting.

Water Fights That Never End

"Without water, the land dies. Without the land, we die." — Ruby Archuleta

In the movie, Joe Mondragon kicks open an irrigation gate to water his dry beanfield in the fictional town of Milagro.

This one act starts a battle that feels incredibly real.

The film centres on the acequia water system—community-managed irrigation channels with roots in Spanish and Native American traditions.

When developer Ladd Devine plans a luxury resort that would take water from local farmers, the film asks a simple but powerful question:

Who should control the water?

  • The people who've lived on the land for generations?
  • Or those with money and political connections?

What makes the film special is showing water as more than just a resource—it's the lifeblood of a community.

David vs. Goliath: Small Town, Big Heart

What makes this underdog story stand out:

  • Real consequences: Characters risk their livelihoods and safety
  • No easy victories: The community struggles, argues, and sometimes falters
  • Personal stakes: Each character has their own reason to fight
  • Authentic setting: New Mexico's landscape becomes a character itself

I love how the movie gives each character a personal stake in the fight:

  • For Joe, it's about feeding his family
  • For Ruby, it's about preserving her community
  • For Amarante, it's about honoring traditions

One scene always gets me: when neighbours gather at Joe's beanfield to protect it.

Simple, yet powerful.

Latino Characters Take Center Stage

When The Milagro Beanfield War came out in 1988, Hollywood rarely showed Latino communities with depth.

This film broke new ground with characters who weren't stereotypes:

  • Ruby Archuleta (Sonia Braga): A fierce, intelligent community leader who happens to be a mechanic
  • Sheriff Bernabe Montoya (Rubén Blades): A man torn between his job and his community
  • Joe Mondragon (Chick Vennera): A reluctant hero whose simple act starts a movement
  • Amarante Cordova (Carlos Riquelme): An elderly man who connects the community to its spiritual roots

These characters have flaws, dreams, and complex motivations. Their cultural identity shapes their lives but doesn't define them entirely.

We care about the water rights issue because we care about these people.

A Touch of Magic

The film's secret ingredient? Magical realism.

Amarante Cordova regularly chats with the angel Coyote (a deceased friend), who watches over the community.

These magical moments aren't just quirky additions—they're essential to the story:

  • They connect the present struggle to cultural traditions
  • They add warmth and humor to a political story
  • They show a worldview where community matters more than profit
  • They create some of the film's most memorable scenes

Redford took a risk bringing magical realism—a storytelling style from Latin American literature—to American cinema.

The gamble paid off.

Redford's Love Letter to the Southwest

Redford's direction shows deep respect for the landscape and culture of northern New Mexico.

Behind-the-scenes dedication:

  • Spent years developing the project despite studio hesitation
  • Insisted on filming on location in New Mexico
  • Incorporated local talent both in front of and behind the camera
  • Balanced political message with compelling storytelling

His camera lingers on:

  • Mountains in golden afternoon light
  • Crystal-clear acequia water flowing through fields
  • Ancient adobe buildings against blue skies
  • Beans sprouting from dry earth

These visuals help us understand why this land is worth fighting for.

More Than Just a Bean Field

Joe's beanfield becomes a powerful symbol throughout the film:

One of my favourite scenes shows the beans finally sprouting. The joy on Joe's face tells us everything about what this field means to him.

It's not just crops; it's dignity.

Timeless Themes in a Specific Setting

While The Milagro Beanfield War is firmly set in northern New Mexico, its themes feel universal:

  • Communities fighting to preserve their way of life
  • The tension between development and tradition
  • Finding courage to stand up to intimidation
  • The power of unlikely alliances
  • The importance of cultural identity

The film frames these big issues through personal stories. We don't just learn about water rights in the abstract—we see what they mean for Joe's family, for Ruby's garage, and for Amarante's home.

5 Most Powerful Moments

  • The first irrigation – When water first flows into Joe's dry field, setting everything in motion
  • Ruby confronting Bloom – Challenging him to use his newspaper to help the community
  • Amarante's standoff – An elderly man facing armed agents with nothing but moral authority
  • The community gathering – Neighbours coming together to protect the beanfield
  • The final celebration – victory that feels earned through collective struggle

Why This Film Still Captures Our Hearts

The Milagro Beanfield War balances hope with realism.

It acknowledges real challenges facing communities but refuses to surrender to cynicism.

What I love most about this film is how it finds beauty in the everyday:

  • A field of beans becomes sacred
  • An irrigation ditch becomes worth fighting for
  • A small town meeting becomes a revolutionary act

As a movie lover, I appreciate how it tells a politically relevant story without sacrificing:

  • Character development
  • Humor
  • Emotional impact
  • Visual beauty

A Different Kind of Hero Story

While Joe Mondragon's action starts the story, the real hero is the community itself.

This ensemble approach feels refreshingly different from typical Hollywood narratives centred on a single heroic individual.

The film shows how change happens when people with different talents work together:

  • Ruby organizes and motivates
  • Amarante provides spiritual guidance
  • Charlie Bloom offers legal expertise
  • Sheriff Montoya quietly resists from within
  • Joe provides the spark with his beanfield

Together, they become something greater than any one person could be.

In today's world of blockbuster spectacles, The Milagro Beanfield War reminds us that powerful stories can come from small places.

It shows that sometimes, the most revolutionary act is simply tending your own garden.

If you haven't seen it, Redford's gem delivers not just a politically relevant story but a thoroughly enjoyable movie experience that will leave you cheering for the underdog.

And that's why it still matters.

This article represents my personal response to a film that continues to inspire with its blend of humour, magical realism, and social commentary. It's a movie that reminds us why we love film—because great stories can entertain us while also making us think.
